paras: The killing of Henry Jefferson was the beating to death of a Black man at Hirsch's wood yard near Houston, Texas, in the summer of 1900, probably in July. Several men described as "negroes" were charged in the killing, and one of them gave a sworn statement describing it. The Houston Daily Post called it a lynching when it reported that a second man, Charles Harris, was held on a murder charge for his alleged part in it.

Jefferson, whom the Post described as "colored," was killed at a wood yard or wood camp owned by a man named Hirsch, given as "Hirsch's wood yard" in the Post and "Hirsh's wood camp near Houston" in the Shiner Gazette. According to the Shiner Gazette, he was beaten to death. Neither paper gives a precise date: the Gazette placed it "a short time since" on 8 August, and the Post "several weeks ago" on 17 August. No reason for the killing and no accusation against Jefferson appear in the coverage.

By early August, W. A. Williams, also known as W. A. Long, was among the men charged with the beating, and he made a sworn statement in which he "detailed how the awful deed was done." Charles Harris, whose race the Post did not give, was charged with murder for "alleged complicity in the lynching" and received a habeas corpus hearing in the criminal district court on Wednesday, 15 August. No report of the result of that hearing, an indictment or a trial was found.

Coverage was slight and appeared only in Texas white papers. The Shiner Gazette carried a single sentence in its "Texanettes" column of state news and identified the accused only as "negroes." The Houston Daily Post mentioned the case only to correct its own court report of the previous day, which had wrongly linked Harris to the murder of Mal Toole. In that correction, printed among other "City Brevities," the Post used the word "lynching," a term the Gazette did not use.
No coverage in the Black press was found.

bases: The Houston Daily Post called the killing 'the lynching of Henry Jefferson' and a second paper said several men were charged with beating him to death (A2, A1).

Jefferson was beaten to death by men later charged with murder, and the local paper called it a lynching (A1, A2); the coverage does not state how many took part beyond 'one of the negroes charged' plus Harris, nor any accusation or motive behind the killing (A1, A2).

Two papers, a Houston daily and a Texas weekly's state-news column, agree that Henry Jefferson was killed at Hirsch's (Hirsh's) wood yard or camp at or near Houston and that more than one man was charged (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Houston Daily Post (local)
accounts.gist: Charles Harris was charged with murder for alleged complicity in the lynching of Henry Jefferson at Hirsch's wood yard several weeks earlier; the paper corrected an earlier report linking him to another murder.

accounts.label: Texas state-news brief
accounts.gist: Several Black men were charged with beating Jefferson to death at Hirsh's wood camp near Houston, and one of them, Williams alias Long, gave a sworn statement on how it was done.

framing.detail: The Houston Post mentioned the case only in a correction within its 'City Brevities' column, calling it 'the lynching of Henry Jefferson, colored'.
The Shiner Gazette ran a one-sentence 'Texanettes' item calling the killing 'the awful deed' and identifying the accused as 'negroes'.

versions.value: a beating to death by men described as 'negroes', with no use of the word lynching

conflicts.note: The accounts do not contradict each other on the core event; they differ in label. The Post, a local paper, used 'lynching'; the Shiner brief named the accused as Black men. Harris's race is not stated.
Probably the same place, with variant spelling and wording.
